newsitem.title: USA: Texas utilities push stranded costs legislation.
newsitem.headline: Texas utilities push stranded costs legislation.

text.p: Eleventh-hour legislation was set to be introduced in the Texas Legislature allowing electric utilities to use excess profits to pay down stranded costs over the next two years, lobbyists said Thursday.

The proposal also would allow the utilities to file plans with the state Public Utility Commission to pay down stranded costs embedded in generating and regulatory assets, according to a draft of the legislation obtained by Reuters.

"The commission may require an electric utility to direct any earnings in excess of its authorized rate of return toward a balance between refunds to customers and reductions in invested capital associated with generating and related regulatory assets," the draft bill said.

With prospects for deregulation of the electric industry dead in this biennial session, utilities were pushing for a bill allowing them to recover potentially millions of dollars in stranded costs over the next two years, lobbyists said.
The bill was backed by the PUC but met with stiff opposition from large industrial customers, Texas electric co-operatives and power marketers, lobbyists said.

The proposal was to be tacked onto a Senate bill now being considered by the House State Affairs committee, the lobbyists said. If it is voted out of the House by this weekend, it would have to return to the Senate for approval, they said.
The legislation was considered a last gasp by electric utilities in the state seeking to avoid rate cuts signalled by the PUC in its recent Central Power & Light Co rate case.
In that case, the commission ordered the utility to cut retail rates by $27 million this year and by $16 million in 1998 and 1999. The utility has sought a rehearing in the case.

Lobbyists said there was little hope a rumored special session of the legislature would be called by Gov. George Bush to revisit electric deregulation if the session ends on June 2 without a bill being passed.
"That's just not going to happen," one lobbyist said.
